item.title: What Is a Prosthetic Arm? A Complete Introduction for New Amputees
item.description:
Prosthetic arms are artificial devices designed to replace missing upper limbs. Modern technology has advanced significantly from older designs, offering devices that mimic natural hand movements, respond to muscle signals, and even provide sensory feedback.

Prevalence

According to a 2024 study, approximately 2.3 million Americans currently live with limb loss, with about 9% involving upper limbs. Common causes include workplace accidents, motor vehicle collisions, vascular disease, and congenital limb differences.

item.title: How Weather Affects Prosthetics: Tips for Managing Seasonal Changes
item.description:
Environmental shifts present distinct challenges for prosthetic users. Warm weather may increase socket tightness, while cold mornings can create stiffness. Rain and snow alter familiar terrain underfoot. These responses reflect a normal give-and-take between body and device rather than equipment failure. Understanding how weather affects your prosthesis can help you maintain comfort and confidence through every seasonal transition.

Does Weather Really Affect Prosthetic Devices?

Temperature fluctuations cause changes in residual limb volume — swelling in heat, shrinking in cold — which directly affects socket fit. Moisture from precipitation and humidity can affect components and skin health over time, though modern prosthetics are built to be durable. Seasonal changes are normal, and prosthetic care is meant to adapt to them.

item.title: Understanding Prosthetics: What to Expect After Limb Loss
item.description:
Limb loss brings both visible and subtle changes to how a person moves, handles daily tasks, and relates to their own body. Exploring prosthetic options for the first time can feel uncertain, and that uncertainty touches both the physical and emotional sides of recovery. At Bionic Prosthetics & Orthotics, we frame prosthetic care as a journey, not a transaction.

What Is a Prosthetic Limb?

A prosthetic limb is a custom medical device that supports movement after limb loss. It can help with walking, reduce strain on the rest of the body, and restore the ability to carry out daily activities — but it cannot replace natural sensation, and it doesn’t work independently of the person wearing it. The goal is not perfection. The goal is progress that holds up in real life.

item.title: From First Steps to the School Dance: Jada's Pediatric AFO Success Story
item.description:
Small Steps, Big Confidence: How an AFO Helped Jada Find Her Rhythm

Jada initially struggled with walking and balance. With the steady support of her foster mother, Dana, she found her way to Bionic Prosthetics & Orthotics’ Joliet clinic. Rather than searching for a quick fix, the family pursued meaningful, ongoing support through orthotic care.

When Walking Feels Like Work

For some children, movement takes conscious effort, and balance has to be learned intentionally rather than developing on its own. As our team puts it, “the goal wasn’t to change who she was. It was to support how she moved.” Jada’s care team recommended a custom AFO (Ankle-Foot Orthosis) — not as a restriction, but as a guide, designed to support proper alignment and reduce physical strain with every step.

item.title: A Day in the Life: Living With a Bionic Limb
item.description:
Individuals who use prosthetic devices carry stories of resilience, humor, adaptation, identity, and quiet victories that no one else sees. This is a look at what it means to live fully with a bionic limb, rather than focusing only on limitation.

Morning Routine: Residual Limb Care

The day typically begins with a specific set of care steps: gentle cleansing and drying, moisturizing during non-wear hours, checking the skin for pressure points, and attaching the liner and socket. This process becomes routine over time, but it can still carry emotional weight — representing either loss or strength, depending on the day and the person.

item.title: Assistive Devices That Complement Your Prosthesis
item.description:
Learning to walk with a prosthesis requires patience, practice, and the right support. For individuals with limb loss, walkers, canes, or crutches serve as temporary tools supporting safe movement during physical adaptation.

Why Assistive Devices Matter

Following amputation, the body develops new patterns of balance, posture, and weight distribution. These devices provide stability during gait training, reduce fall risk, improve alignment and weight-bearing tolerance, and build confidence in prosthetic function. As the saying goes, they’re there in the beginning to help you cross safely, not to stay forever.

item.title: Understanding Cranial Helmets: Supporting Healthy Head Growth in Babies
item.description: Every baby develops at their own pace, but during the early months of life, a baby’s skull remains soft and flexible — which is completely natural and necessary for healthy brain growth. Sometimes this flexibility results in flat spots or uneven head shaping, a condition known as plagiocephaly. A cranial remolding helmet, also called a cranial orthosis, is a safe, lightweight device that gently encourages a baby’s skull to grow into a more symmetrical shape. At Bionic Prosthetics & Orthotics, our team works closely with families to support this process from evaluation through follow-up care.

item.title: Residual Limb Care: Your Guide to Comfort, Confidence & Healing
item.description:
Why Residual Limb Care Matters

Following amputation, the residual limb faces new pressures from prosthetic sockets, friction from liners, and shifts in skin moisture and tissue volume. Poor care practices can result in irritation, blisters, or skin breakdown, which can limit comfortable prosthesis use. In fact, 60–70% of prosthetic users report at least one episode of skin irritation or pressure discomfort within their first year of use.

item.title: Sports & Prosthetics: How Athletes with Limb Loss Break Barriers Every Day
item.description: Sports transcend mere physical activity — they represent self-expression, identity, confidence, and freedom. For individuals with limb loss, adaptive sports provide a powerful avenue to reclaim movement and discover new capabilities within their own bodies. Modern advancements in bionic prosthetics and orthotics enable athletes around the world to participate in running, cycling, swimming, climbing, and competitive events of all kinds. Bionic Prosthetics & Orthotics supports athletes of every age and ability level in returning to the sports they love, or discovering new ones.

item.title: When Do I Need a Follow-Up for My Prosthesis?
item.description:
Many patients hesitate to schedule follow-up appointments, assuming they’re only necessary when something goes wrong. But follow-ups aren’t just for when something goes wrong — think of them like routine maintenance for your car: skipping them doesn’t save you trouble in the long run, it just delays the discovery of small issues before they become big ones.

Why Follow-Ups Matter

Regular follow-up visits offer several key benefits:

  • Spotting issues early, before they become painful or limit mobility
  • Adjusting the device for optimal fit as your body changes
  • Tracking your progress over time
  • Providing expert guidance tailored to your specific needs

Bodies change over time — through weight fluctuations, activity level changes, muscle development, and more — making ongoing professional support essential to keeping your prosthesis working the way it should.

item.title: Phantom Pain: Understanding and Managing Phantom Limb Sensation
item.description:
What Is Phantom Limb Pain?

Phantom limb pain refers to the sensation of pain in a limb that has been amputated. Despite the absence of the limb, the brain continues to receive signals from the nerves that originally served the lost limb. This phenomenon can cause discomfort, ranging from mild to severe pain, and can be a significant challenge for amputees.

item.title: The Importance of Physical Therapy for Amputees
item.description:
A Fresh Start, One Step at a Time

Losing a limb transforms everything, yet recovery remains possible. The journey to recovery begins with a good physical therapy program. This foundational phase prepares individuals for prosthetic use while facilitating renewed strength and autonomy.

What Physical Therapy Really Does for You

Therapy following amputation extends beyond wound healing — it addresses comprehensive rehabilitation. Whether it’s improving balance, building strength, or getting your body ready to use a prosthesis, therapy helps you step back into your world with confidence.

item.title: What Is Gait Training and How Can It Help After Amputation?
item.description:
Gait training is an important component of a physical therapy program designed to help people walk more efficiently, safely, and confidently, especially after amputation. The therapy strengthens muscles and joints, enhances posture and balance, decreases fall risk, and rebuilds endurance.

Understanding Compensatory Movements

A key concept in gait training is compensatory movements — unintended body adjustments amputees may develop to reduce pain, address muscle weakness, or prevent falls. While minor gait variations are normal, excessive compensation can negatively affect walking confidence, comfort, and energy use.

item.title: Preventing Muscle Contractures After Amputation
item.description:
What Are Contractures, and Why Do They Matter?

Contractures develop when the muscles and tissues around the amputation site tighten, limiting the movement of the remaining limb. This condition can be painful and can make it much harder to use a lower limb prosthesis effectively. Maintaining range of motion in the residual limb and the surrounding joints supports a natural gait and reduces the energy a person has to expend during everyday activities.

item.title: Spring Cleaning Your Prosthesis: Maintenance Tips
item.description:
As spring arrives, amputees benefit from seasonal maintenance routines for their prosthetics. Beyond typical household cleaning, a consistent prosthesis cleansing routine can prevent inflammation, irritation, and infection as warmer weather approaches.

Clean Your Liner Every Night

The prosthetic liner provides a secure fit while absorbing sweat moisture. Daily cleaning is essential, preferably at night to allow adequate drying time.

  • Dampen a soft cloth with warm (not hot) water and wring it out thoroughly to prevent excess moisture.
  • Use mild, fragrance-free soap, rubbing alcohol, prosthesis-specific soaps, mild dish soap, or gentle body wash. Always consult your prosthetist and perform a skin spot test before using new products.
  • Allow the liner to dry completely in a cool, dry space before reinserting.

Clean Your Device Regularly

All prosthetic components require regular cleaning, including the sock and socket.

item.title: Prosthetic vs Prosthesis: What's the Difference and Why It Matters
item.description:
Terminology around prosthetic devices often causes confusion, even among patients who have worn one for years. The core distinction is simple: “prosthesis” refers to the physical device itself, while “prosthetic” serves as a descriptive adjective. For example, a patient might say “I wear a prosthetic leg,” using the adjective form in casual speech.

A prosthesis is the actual medical device that replaces a missing body part, and clinical documentation typically uses this term. Conversely, “prosthetic” describes items related to the device — such as a prosthetic socket, prosthetic care, or prosthetic fitting.

item.title: What to Know About Your First Prosthetic Leg: A Beginner's Guide
item.description:
Getting a first prosthetic leg can feel overwhelming. Most people don’t arrive with clear expectations. They arrive with questions, mixed emotions, and a quiet hope that daily life might start feeling easier again.

What a Prosthetic Leg Is

A prosthetic leg is a custom medical device for individuals missing part or all of a leg due to injury, illness, or birth conditions. These devices support movement, improve stability, and help reduce physical and mental fatigue. Most prosthetic legs consist of multiple parts, including a socket, support structure, and foot or knee components.

item.title: Bionic Patients and Team Shine at AOPA 2024: A Journey of Learning and Innovation
item.description:
In September, members of the Bionic team attended the American Orthotic & Prosthetic Association (AOPA) Conference in Charlotte, North Carolina. The event provided educational courses, product demonstrations, and networking opportunities for the clinical team to enhance their expertise and learn about recent developments in the orthotics and prosthetics field.

Two long-time Bionic patients, Reynaldo Morales and Raymond Conley, both above-knee amputees, participated in the conference for the first time. This marked the first instance of Bionic patients attending an O&P conference alongside the company’s clinical team.

item.title: Bionic's Brad Watson Named to NAAOP Board of Directors
item.description:
L. Bradley Watson, a Regional Manager and Certified Prosthetist & Orthotist at Bionic, has been elected to the board of directors of the National Association for the Advancement of Orthotics and Prosthetics (NAAOP). Watson brings more than 35 years of experience in the field to this new role.

NAAOP Board President Ann Leimkuehler Moss welcomed Watson to the board, noting his extensive background, including his previous and current roles on the BOC board and the Kentucky state licensure board.

item.title: Limb Loss and Limb Difference Awareness Month
item.description:
Key Statistics

More than 500 individuals in the United States experience limb loss every day, and projections suggest the population living with limb loss could nearly double by 2050. Today, more than 2.7 million people across the country are navigating life with limb loss or limb difference, and this reality touches individuals across every demographic.

About LLLDAM

Limb Loss and Limb Difference Awareness Month was established in 2011 by the Amputee Coalition and takes place every April. The initiative aims to amplify voices, giving affected individuals the space to share their personal journeys while advancing education and advocacy for the broader community.

item.title: 9 Questions You Need to Ask Your Prosthetist or Orthotist
item.description:
Appointments with your prosthetics or orthotics specialist offer real opportunities to enhance mobility, reduce pain, and improve overall quality of life. Getting the most out of these visits depends on asking informed questions and advocating for yourself. Here are nine essential questions to bring to your next appointment.

1. Experience with Your Condition

Ask about the clinician’s specific experience treating patients with your type of amputation or your particular mobility needs. Expertise can vary quite a bit from case to case.

item.title: Tony Gutierrez: Growing with Bionic
item.description:
Tony Gutierrez joined Bionic in 2014 at the Tinley Park, Illinois office after leaving a competitor focused primarily on revenue. He sought an organization that would foster his professional development with clear advancement pathways.

“I was given a yearly revenue goal with a plan to reach salary bonuses and an open path to reach it, but it was up to me to develop my referral sources,” he explains. Initial marketing challenges shifted once he recognized that patient advocacy and clinical team communication constituted effective practice-building.

item.title: The Bionic Difference: Alexander Lecher
item.description:
Alexander Lecher is an unstoppable young child who loves playing with stuffed animals, riding his balance bike, exploring outdoors, and visiting playgrounds — despite having a full foot prosthesis.

Macrodactyly & Syme’s Amputation

Alexander was born with macrodactyly, a congenital condition causing abnormal overgrowth of bones and soft tissue in fingers or toes. Pain from this condition necessitated a full-foot amputation in April 2020 when he was just two years old. The procedure, called a Syme’s amputation, involves removing all foot bones and transferring the heel pad to support the leg bones, preserving leg structure while enabling weight-bearing and comfort.

item.title: The Bionic Difference: Peter Morrison
item.description:
Peter Morrison’s life revolved around horses. Riding horseback, caring for his animals, and competing in events far and wide represented his passion. However, an accident during his early morning commute threatened to permanently alter his highly active lifestyle.

Peter’s truck hit a tree and overturned, becoming severely crushed. His left leg sustained multiple fractures. After doctors spent over a week attempting to save the limb, they determined amputation was necessary to preserve his life and performed a below-knee amputation.

item.title: The Bionic Difference: Reynaldo Morales
item.description:
Reynaldo Morales loves basketball. Growing up in Gary, Indiana, taught him a love for the court and the community that forms around it that has followed him for his entire life. But on the morning of April 12th, 2007, a car accident threatened to take that away. Now, Reynaldo is back on the courts and still flashing his winning smile.

“I was always an active kid,” Reynaldo says, hardly able to keep from smiling as he recounts the story. “I used to do backflips as early as 2nd grade and I went to Lisa’s Gymnastics in 3rd to really sharpen my skills… but basketball was my true sport.”
